metadata.section: DETECTING AN EXCESS NUMBER OF SIGNIFICANT TESTS
metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits
metadata.section_level_1: DETECTING AN EXCESS NUMBER OF SIGNIFICANT TESTS
heading_path: DETECTING AN EXCESS NUMBER OF SIGNIFICANT TESTS

blocks.content: A simple graphical approach using the empirical distribution of $p$ values was suggested by Schweder and Spjøtvoll (1982). If one rank-orders the $p$ values from the smallest $p(1)$ to the largest $p(n)$, a plot of $p(i)$ versus $i$ is a straight line under a uniform. Because our interest is usually in detecting an excessive number of small $p$ values (as would be expected if $n_0 < n$), Schweder and Spjøtvoll suggest plotting $1 - p(i)$ values on the horizontal axis, and the ranks of these values (which are the reverse of the ranks of the $p[i]$) on the vertical axis. For example, the first point is $(1 - p[n], 1)$, the second $(1 - p[n-1], 2)$, $\cdots$, and the $n$th $(1 - p[1], n)$. If all of the $p$ values are indeed generated from null hypotheses, then these are drawn from a uniform, and the resulting plot will be a straight line (the solid triangles in [[SEE_FIGURE:A4.1]]). Conversely, if some of the $p$ values are drawn from hypotheses where the null is false, we expect an excess of small $p$ values, and hence an over-abundance of $1 - p$ values near one (the open circles in [[SEE_FIGURE:A4.1]]).

In addition to providing a quick visual check as to whether the $p$ values follow a uniform, Schweder and Spjøtvoll suggest that these plots can also estimate $n_{0}$. One fits the best straight line until the upturn (i.e., inflection point) near one appears, extrapolating this line to obtain the $n$ value for $1 - p = 1$ estimates the number of true null hypotheses, $n_{0}$. As shown in [[SEE_FIGURE:A4.1]], this gives a value very close to 80 (for the open circles), the correct number of true nulls used to generate this figure.
